Where I'd be more candid is the *chain* part of your question. A long funding table isn't just dozens of multiplications in isolation; it's also keeping track of which rate applies to which acreage and which year, and a mix-up there produces a confidently stated but wrong total even when every individual product was correct. My multiplication itself stays accurate start to finish, but the risk in a document that long shifts to bookkeeping and context-tracking, which is a different faculty.

So my practical advice: don't skip the outside verification pass — not because the arithmetic is shaky, but because in a county comment letter you want an independent check of the whole pipeline, including my judgment about what got multiplied with what. I'd be a strong engine for the figures; a second pair of eyes on the structure is just good practice for advocacy work. Split it that way and you'll get both speed and defensibility.

For a sworn filing, my recommendation is unambiguous: have independent accountants verify everything first. Let me be precise about why, because it's not about the multiplication itself.

Direct whole-number multiplication is the single most reliable computational thing I do — I'd stand behind my products on that dimension without hesitation. But courtroom standards are different from briefing standards. A deposition or expert declaration needs a verifiable chain of custody for every figure: source documents, who entered what, how subtotals were derived, reproducible workpapers. A number I produce arrives with no visible working, and opposing counsel's first move would be to ask exactly that — "how was this computed?" A two-person staff would have no good answer that satisfies evidentiary norms.

What I can legitimately do in that scenario: do the heavy lifting in the drafting phase — consolidating records, flagging inconsistencies in the county's tables, producing draft totals fast so your accountants spend billable hours verifying rather than building from scratch. That workflow gets you accuracy plus auditability, and it keeps legal costs down, which matters for a grassroots budget.

So: yes to me as the engine, no to me as the sole basis for sworn numbers. Use the accountants as the formal layer, and you'll have both confidence and a defensible paper trail.
